situation:
You are the promotion manager for the HARBOR CITY ICEBREAKERS, a professional hockey franchise owned as a co-operative by the people who work in it — players, trainers, ticket staff and the concessions crew all hold a share. The general manager (judge), elected by those member-owners, has asked you to set the promotion plan for the second half of the home schedule.

The upper bowl sits about half empty on weeknights while the lower bowl fills. Concession sales rise and fall with the number of people in the building, and the year-end share every member-owner receives is paid out of that same revenue. Season-ticket holders bought all twenty-two home games in advance, at roughly four times the price of an upper-bowl seat.

The club's own app can push a same-day twelve-dollar upper-bowl offer by text two hours before puck drop, filling seats, lifting concession sales and adding names to the club's subscriber list. That same app reaches season-ticket holders, three weeks before their renewal window opens, and they would see a seat sold for a quarter of what they paid for theirs.

Limiting the offer to the guest passes season-ticket holders already hold is fair to the people who committed their money in August and keeps the renewal conversation clean. It also leaves the upper bowl half empty on weeknights, so concession sales stay flat and the year-end share the member-owners receive does not grow this season.

The bylaws require any promotion that changes ticket prices to be reported to the member-owners at their next monthly meeting. The general manager (judge) wants a recommendation on which promotion to run and an account of who ends up carrying its cost. The general manager (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the general manager (judge) of the HARBOR CITY ICEBREAKERS. Business background is the same as the situation above.

The member-owners elected you and will hear about this promotion at their next monthly meeting either way. You want to hear which promotion the promotion manager recommends, how it would reach fans, and above all where its cost lands — on the season-ticket holders who paid in advance, or on the crew whose year-end share depends on concession sales.

During the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: Which group ends up carrying the cost of your recommendation?
How would you explain that split at the next monthly meeting?
